name: GrapheneOS
summary: A privacy and security-hardened mobile operating system based on the Android Open Source Project (AOSP), featuring a hardened memory allocator, kernel exploit mitigations, Sandboxed Google Play compatibility layer, and exclusive support for Google Pixel hardware.
license: GPLv2 (Linux kernel) / Apache License 2.0 & MIT (userspace components)

content.introduction: GrapheneOS is a free and open-source mobile operating system focused on defensive security engineering and user privacy. Developed as a direct hardened downstream fork of the Android Open Source Project (AOSP), it integrates substantial low-level architectural mitigations designed to prevent and contain software exploit techniques while preserving compatibility with mainstream Android applications.
content.what_is_it: GrapheneOS is a production mobile operating system targeting modern Google Pixel devices. It eliminates Google telemetry, proprietary services, and tracking identifiers by default, while replacing critical AOSP userspace and kernel subsystems with heavily hardened equivalents, including a custom memory allocator, enhanced address space layout randomization, and fine-grained hardware permission controls.
content.exploit_mitigations_and_kernel_hardening: At the core system level, GrapheneOS replaces Android's standard memory allocator with `hardened_malloc`, a specialized security-focused allocator engineered by Daniel Micay. `hardened_malloc` implements fine-grained slab quarantining, guard pages, address space randomization, and out-of-line metadata to actively detect and neutralize heap corruption, use-after-free, and double-free vulnerabilities before they can be weaponized. On supported modern ARMv9 hardware, GrapheneOS activates hardware-based Memory Tagging Extension (MTE) in synchronous mode, providing architectural memory safety enforcement at near-native speeds. The operating system enforces strict W^X (Write XOR Execute) memory policies across user-space binaries and system services, hardens the Bionic C library, eliminates dynamic code generation in sensitive contexts, and applies extensive kernel patches to restrict debug interfaces, system call access, and information leaks.
content.sandboxed_google_play_architecture: Rather than integrating proprietary Google Mobile Services into the privileged system partition or relying on insecure framework-level signature spoofing, GrapheneOS developed the Sandboxed Google Play compatibility layer. Under this architectural paradigm, Google Play Services, the Google Play Store, and Google Services Framework execute strictly as standard, unprivileged user applications within standard Android sandboxes. They possess no special permissions, cannot access device identifiers (such as IMEI, serial numbers, or MAC addresses), and can have network access, location permissions, and file access revoked at any time. Inter-process communication (IPC) calls made by dependent third-party applications are redirected through compatibility shims, allowing banking apps, proprietary messengers, and push notification services to function reliably without compromising the operating system's security architecture.
content.privacy_controls_and_hardware_attestatio: GrapheneOS incorporates granular privacy controls unavailable in stock Android. These include per-app Network and Sensors toggles, allowing users to cut off internet connectivity or sensor tracking (gyroscope, accelerometer) from individual applications without breaking their offline functionality. It features Storage Scopes and Contact Scopes, which provide applications with isolated, user-selected subsets of files or address books instead of granting broad file system permissions. For platform integrity, GrapheneOS includes the open-source Auditor app and remote attestation service, which cryptographically verifies the authenticity of the installed firmware, bootloader locking state, and patch level using the device's hardware security element (Titan M2 or Tensor security core). An automated inactivity reboot timer forces the device back into Before First Unlock (BFU) state, encrypting data at rest if left unattended.
content.hardware_compatibility_and_update_model: GrapheneOS strictly limits its hardware support to Google Pixel smartphones and tablets. This hardware exclusivity is dictated by rigorous technical prerequisites: mandatory support for verified boot with user-installed custom public keys, dedicated hardware security chips (Titan M/M2) with StrongBox keystores, and timely monthly vendor security patches spanning 5 to 7 years. GrapheneOS tracks upstream AOSP releases and distributes monthly security updates via an encrypted, signed over-the-air (OTA) update system.
content.project_origin_release_tagging_and_insta: GrapheneOS was founded as an open-source project in 2014 and was previously known as CopperheadOS; the project states that it will remain a non-profit organisation independent of any single company. Releases are not numbered but tagged with a UTC timestamp: the changelog lists 2026101600 as its most recent entry, dated 16 October 2026. Each build moves through an Alpha channel, then a Beta channel, then the Stable channel once tested by Beta users. Updates are automatic and over the air, sent as delta packages where available, with signature verification and downgrade protection enforced in the update client, in recovery and by verified boot. Initial installation uses factory images verifiable with OpenSSH, through either the WebUSB installer recommended for most users or a command-line procedure that avoids trusting the project's server infrastructure.
content.release_channels_and_rollout_model: Releases are tested by the developers and then pushed to the Alpha channel; the same build is pushed to the Beta channel shortly afterwards, and to the Stable channel once Beta users have exercised it. When problems are caught during Beta testing, a new release is issued through the Beta channel to replace the aborted one. The project notes that downgrading is generally not possible unless a downgrade package has been generated, and that users who cannot tolerate temporary issues should stay on the Stable channel.
content.signature_verification_and_downgrade_pro: Update integrity rests on several layers. Update packages are signed with a release key, the internal payload used by update_engine is signed as well, and verified boot together with the hardware-backed keystore acts as a final layer. According to the project, this combination provides signature verification and downgrade protection for the update path.
content.official_device_list_and_support_windows: Official builds target a named list of Pixel models, each identified by its codename - for example Pixel 6 (oriole), Pixel 8 (shiba), Pixel 9 (tokay) and Pixel Tablet (tangorpro). The project explains that device-specific work on hardware, firmware and drivers is central to its security model, and that supporting a broad set of devices would run directly counter to its goals. Official updates for Pixels typically end shortly after the end of the minimum guaranteed update support, and the FAQ publishes the support end date for each model, for example March 2033 for the Pixel 10a with seven years of guaranteed support. Extended support releases are issued as a stopgap when an OEM stops shipping security updates, without being able to provide full patches.
content.source_repositories_and_component_projec: The project publishes its work as a set of separate repositories rather than a single tree. The organisation account lists the platform manifest used to assemble the operating system, the hardened_malloc allocator - described as usable outside Android as a dynamic library on musl and glibc systems - and the issue tracker for the Android Open Source Project hardening work. Standalone components such as Auditor and AttestationServer keep their own dedicated trackers, which separates the operating system work from the auxiliary services built around it.
content.build_tagging_and_security_patch_cadence: Builds are tagged with the publication date rather than with a semantic version: the current tag is `2026101600`, preceded by `2026100600` and `2026100200`, three builds of the same month, and the changelog lists roughly a hundred tags per year. Each entry names the devices covered and states the Android security patch level it carries - the `2026100600` build brings the full 2026-10-05 patch level together with the October 2026 firmware and hardware abstraction layers for Pixel devices. Kernel updates are tracked per branch rather than per release: the changelog records revisions applied to the 6.1 and 6.12 GKI LTS branches separately, so a device on the older branch can receive a kernel revision while a newer device moves on the other branch. The same entries list the CVEs addressed, and the project publishes separate security preview releases for patches it considers before the monthly Android bulletin.
content.install_prerequisites_and_boot_chain_ver: The command-line installation path documents the constraints as explicitly as the steps. The host computer needs at least 2 GB of free memory and 32 GB of free storage, the phone must not be a carrier variant because a non-zero carrier identifier can disable OEM unlocking, and the flashing tool is checked before use: `fastboot --version` must report at least 35.0.1, and the guide gives 35.0.2-12147458 as the version shipped by the current standalone platform-tools. Unlocking is performed with `fastboot flashing unlock`, which requires a physical confirmation and wipes the device; the bootloader is locked again at the end with `fastboot flashing lock`. Verification after installation does not rely on the installer: the device displays its verified boot key hash, which the user compares against the hash published per Pixel model, and the project notes that Pixel 5 and earlier show only the first 32 bits of that hash while Pixel 6 and later show it in full. Returning to the stock OS requires erasing the custom key with `fastboot erase avb_custom_key`.
advantages: Advanced defensive security posture featuring hardened_malloc, ARMv9 MTE support, and kernel exploit mitigations
Sandboxed Google Play compatibility layer enabling app functionality without granting privileged system access
Granular privacy controls including per-app Network toggles, Sensors toggles, Storage Scopes, and Contact Scopes
Cryptographic hardware-based remote attestation using the Auditor app and Titan M2 security element
Rapid integration of upstream Android Security Bulletin (ASB) patches and quarterly platform updates
disadvantages: Strict hardware limitation exclusively supporting supported Google Pixel devices
Apps relying on mandatory hardware-backed Google Play Integrity verdicts may fail or require configuration
Hardened memory allocation and exploit mitigations can expose bugs in poorly written third-party native code
who_is_it_for: Security engineers, investigative journalists, and privacy-conscious users seeking maximal mobile device hardening
Organizations and professionals requiring cryptographic verification of mobile operating system integrity
Users wanting to run Android applications without granting ambient system privileges to proprietary Google services
who_is_it_not_for: Users wishing to install an operating system on hardware from manufacturers other than Google Pixel
Consumers requiring pre-configured proprietary Google Mobile Services and automated cloud backup accounts out of the box
content.verdict: GrapheneOS represents a benchmark in mobile operating system security engineering. By combining deep kernel and memory allocator hardening with an unprivileged compatibility layer for Google Play services, it achieves a high degree of defensive isolation on Google Pixel hardware without severing access to the broader Android application ecosystem.
